data.text:
Sa Totoo Lang debut is straight FIRE 🔥 Atty. Rowena Guanzon, Cathy Binag (Mama Bing), and guest Prof. Malou Tiquia didn't hold back on Pres. Bongbong Marcos's UN trip to the Commission on Women while the Philippines burns with crises at home.

Key bombshells from the segment:

• “When there is a crisis, the leader needs to be at home, he needs to be taking care of the problems here.” (Prof. Tiquia) — But BBM jets off on a private plane instead?

• OFWs stranded in the Middle East, families worried sick, no swift repatriation from Manila. Meanwhile: “Singapore and Spain have already sent planes... But did we see an employee say, ‘Go ahead and report whoever you want to report. We don’t have any money.’ Manila is not sending anything.” Brutal contrast.

• Pre-departure luxury:  A party in Malacañang right before he left. Hosts call it “insensitive.” Prof. Tiquia drops the classic: “Before he flew away, they had a party... it seems like that’s what they said, ‘Rome is burning.’ Are you having a party?... who spent the money and if it wasn’t the government that spent the money, why did you have a party inside Malacanang?”

• Priorities roasted: Speech on women’s rights (from a leader “not known for women’s advocacy”), pushing for UN Security Council seat, all while fuel prices spike, inflation hits, deficit grows to P17T, panic buying looms, and citizens suffer. “Are you saying that he is running away from the problems that will arise in the Philippines? Yes, he really runs...”

This isn’t just commentary — it’s a wake-up call. Tone-deaf leadership while Rome burns? Nero would be proud. 

Let us burn the place… hahahahaha 😈 (in the name of truth and accountability, of course)

Ano sa tingin niyo, mga kababayan? Priorities ba talaga ‘to? Drop your thoughts below. 🇵🇭

data.text:
Ever wondered why commuting across the Philippines still revolves around roads? It wasn’t always that way, because Manila once ran electric streetcars through a network known as the Tranvia, operated by the Manila Electric Railroad and Light Company and considered one of Asia’s most advanced tram systems before World War II.

Much of that infrastructure was destroyed during the war, and while passenger trains continued under what became Philippine National Railways, national transport priorities gradually shifted toward highways and road vehicles. Jeepneys spread quickly because they were cheap and flexible, while rail expansion slowed and the country grew more dependent on roads even as traffic congestion began costing the economy billions of pesos each day.

Follow @PGMNofficial if you enjoy exploring how the Philippines once moved and why the future of transport may still be waiting on the rails.
